Around 1700 editions of the Wairarapa Times-Age from 1944 to1950 are now accessible from anywhere in the world, following the Wairarapa Archives’ involvement in the National Library of New Zealand’s Collaborative Newspaper Digitisation Programme.

The Archive secured a spot in the programme in May last year, and after Masterton District Library received $5500 in funding from Masterton Trust Lands Trust, the digitisation project is now complete with the newspapers available through the National Library’s Papers Past website.

The digitised 1944-1950 Times-Age editions, comprising nearly 15,000 pages, join editions from 1938 to June 1944. Papers Past also includes digitised copes of the Times-Age’s predecessors, the Wairarapa Age and Wairarapa Daily Times.

Masterton District Council’s Content and Access Manager Stephnie Burton says it is exciting to see the newspapers made available online.

“This work is a key part of not only preserving Wairarapa’s history, but also making it more accessible to anyone who wants to learn more,” she said.

“It’s been a significant project over the past year, so it’s incredibly rewarding to now see it live and available to the public.”

The programme provides partial funding to support the digitisation of newspapers across Aotearoa New Zealand. Preserving newspapers is especially important, as older editions were often the primary source of news and information, documenting the people, places, and events that have shaped community identity.

“Physical newspapers become more fragile over time. Digitising them not only preserves this content for future generations, but also makes it far more accessible, not just locally, but globally,” Burton says.

“The Archive receives research requests from all over the world, so making our collections available online is a huge step forward.

“We are also very grateful to Masterton Trust Lands Trust for their funding support, which has made this project possible.”

Following robust discussion at an extraordinary Masterton District Council meeting, elected members have agreed to reduce the proposed average rates increase to 4.2 percent for the next financial year.

Mayor Bex Johnson welcomed the decision.

“Elected members were clear in their desire to explore options to bring the rates increase down, and we’re pleased to see that work reflected in today’s decision,” Mayor Johnson said.
“We know many in our community are doing it tough. Our focus has been on balancing essential services and priorities for the next 12 months while keeping costs as low as possible.”

The Council considered three options: retaining the previously proposed 5.2 percent increase, which was already below the original Annual Plan figure, or moving to a 4 percent increase through a combination of cost savings and revenue adjustments.

After strong discussion and deliberation, an amended version of the second option was agreed. These amendments excluded some of the proposed cost saving measures.

Mayor Johnson said achieving the lower increase required careful trade-offs.

“We’ve had to be very prudent with the budget to identify savings. This includes looking at increased revenue from user-pays services and reducing expenditure in several areas. While we want to reduce costs as much as possible, we don’t want to just kick the can down the road, and we need to ensure we are investing appropriately in our community and infrastructure.”

She noted that the revised budget fundamentally meets the requirements of the Local Government Act.

“We remain committed to keeping operating costs as low as possible while continuing to deliver core services.”

A sweeping panorama of more than 500 dots, most provided by the community, features in Masterton District Library’s effort to repeat its success as national winner of the Out on the Shelves display competition.

The competition is part of an annual campaign in June celebrating rainbow (LGBTQIA+) literature in libraries across New Zealand.

The library won first place in the 2025, and library assistant Danielle Stark said the inspiration for the rainbow display this year was the book, The Dot, by Peter H. Reynolds, and its theme of “making our mark and seeing where it takes us”.

Danielle contacted a range of groups for dots, including early childhood centres, IDEA services, English for speakers of other languages programmes (ESOL), and councils.

“So many people took up the challenge, some completing the mission with multiple additions, sometimes daily. They really let out their creative flair and came up with amazing results!”

Library manager Tiffany Rawlings said the entry was a real community effort.

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Future of Local Government community survey results

Masterton District Council’s recent Future of Local Government Survey has seen the Masterton community clearly signalling that the Council should take advantage of the Government’s Head Start pathway to amalgamation but ensure it is good value for money and that a strong local voice is priority.

More than ninety four percent of respondents to the survey supported the Council leading its own reform, rather than waiting for a government-imposed outcome.

Value for money was the highest priority residents identified, narrowly ahead of the quality of infrastructure and services, with strong themes running through the survey around keeping decisions and community-facing services local where possible, and ensuring any change works to improve affordability.

Mayor Bex Johnson thanked Mastertonians for their clear input.

"Our community has told us what they want, and they have not been shy about it. The job now is to take everything people told us, including affordability and protecting core services, and make the best call we can for our district. Local matters to us, but local at any cost is not what people have asked for. They want value for money.

“Affordability with local decision making will be the test we hold every option against."

The survey drew 559 submissions, with Mayor Johnson emphasising that it was a genuine effort to understand community priorities, not a binding vote.

"I firmly believe it was important to hear our community’s priorities early. Having the views of our community at the table and understanding what matters most to them will be a key part of our discussions.”

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Spruce-up for CBD through Town Centre Improvement Fund 🌟 

A total of 11 Queen Street businesses have been approved for funding support from Masterton District Council to cover up to 80 percent of the cost of improving the look of their buildings.

The $200K Town Centre Improvement Fund was made available to businesses with a postal address on Queen Street and eligible side streets between Chapel Street and Dixon Street.

Projects receiving funding support include repainting shopfronts, fixing verandahs, upgrading lighting, restoring heritage features, and improving building façades.

Businesses and properties receiving support are:
👉  Hells Pizza - exterior painting
👉  Paper Plus - replacement lighting
👉  Gadget Guru – verandah fixes
👉  Hedley’s Bookshop - restoration of front canopy and replacement lighting
👉  Bear Flag Books - shopfront painting
👉  Master Fried Chicken - painting of shop frontage
👉  Wairarapa Bakery and Café, Annapurna - repainting of front verandah
👉  Studio 8 Interiors - façade improvements
👉  Edge Property for CML Building (corner Perry/Queen Streets) - repainting and remediation of façade
👉  Katipo Holdings (former Hannah’s building, corner Bannister/Queen Streets) - façade upgrade, including cladding and verandah upgrades
👉  10 O’Clock Cookie Company - modernise outside structure with a louvre system

Applications were assessed by the Town Centre Scrum, made up of mana whenua, local trusts, and business representatives.

The final allocation was decided by the Chief Executive of Masterton District Council <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/kymfell?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Kym Fell</a>.

“The Town Centre Improvement Fund is helping to accelerate improvements that might otherwise take years to achieve, creating a more attractive, vibrant, and welcoming environment for residents, visitors, and businesses alike,” Mr Fell said.

“What is particularly pleasing is that this investment complements the significant infrastructure work currently underway in Queen Street. As we renew the assets beneath the ground, we’re also helping to improve what people see above it, ensuring the benefits are both practical and visible.”

Masterton Mayor Bex Johnson said the fund signalled the Council’s commitment to supporting local business.

“Investing in our businesses means investing in our community and creating the town we want to live in.

“The current water main replacement project is giving the CBD a much-needed refresh. These extra improvements will make our place somewhere we can be proud of.”

Businesses have up to 12 months to complete projects, with funding released once the work is finished and signed off.

A second round of funding may be considered later in the year.</p>

Around 1700 editions of the Wairarapa Times-Age from 1944 to1950 are now accessible from anywhere in the world, following the Wairarapa Archives’ involvement in the National Library of New Zealand’s Collaborative Newspaper Digitisation Programme.

The Archive secured a spot in the programme in May last year, and after Masterton District Library received $5500 in funding from Masterton Trust Lands Trust, the digitisation project is now complete with the newspapers available through the National Library’s Papers Past website.

The digitised 1944-1950 Times-Age editions, comprising nearly 15,000 pages, join editions from 1938 to June 1944. Papers Past also includes digitised copes of the Times-Age’s predecessors, the Wairarapa Age and Wairarapa Daily Times.

Masterton District Council’s Content and Access Manager Stephnie Burton says it is exciting to see the newspapers made available online.

“This work is a key part of not only preserving Wairarapa’s history, but also making it more accessible to anyone who wants to learn more,” she said.

“It’s been a significant project over the past year, so it’s incredibly rewarding to now see it live and available to the public.”

The programme provides partial funding to support the digitisation of newspapers across Aotearoa New Zealand. Preserving newspapers is especially important, as older editions were often the primary source of news and information, documenting the people, places, and events that have shaped community identity.

“Physical newspapers become more fragile over time. Digitising them not only preserves this content for future generations, but also makes it far more accessible, not just locally, but globally,” Burton says.

“The Archive receives research requests from all over the world, so making our collections available online is a huge step forward.

“We are also very grateful to Masterton Trust Lands Trust for their funding support, which has made this project possible.”

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Average 4.2% rates rise agreed following savings, service adjustments

Following robust discussion at an extraordinary Masterton District Council meeting, elected members have agreed to reduce the proposed average rates increase to 4.2 percent for the next financial year.

Mayor Bex Johnson welcomed the decision.

“Elected members were clear in their desire to explore options to bring the rates increase down, and we’re pleased to see that work reflected in today’s decision,” Mayor Johnson said.
“We know many in our community are doing it tough. Our focus has been on balancing essential services and priorities for the next 12 months while keeping costs as low as possible.”

The Council considered three options: retaining the previously proposed 5.2 percent increase, which was already below the original Annual Plan figure, or moving to a 4 percent increase through a combination of cost savings and revenue adjustments.

After strong discussion and deliberation, an amended version of the second option was agreed. These amendments excluded some of the proposed cost saving measures.

Mayor Johnson said achieving the lower increase required careful trade-offs.

“We’ve had to be very prudent with the budget to identify savings. This includes looking at increased revenue from user-pays services and reducing expenditure in several areas. While we want to reduce costs as much as possible, we don’t want to just kick the can down the road, and we need to ensure we are investing appropriately in our community and infrastructure.”

She noted that the revised budget fundamentally meets the requirements of the Local Government Act.

“We remain committed to keeping operating costs as low as possible while continuing to deliver core services.”

The updated average rates increase will be formally adopted alongside the Annual Plan on 24 June.</p>
